blocks.en: 1. The Fourth Witness: The Ground Itself
blocks.es_reference: 1. El Cuarto Testigo: La Tierra Misma

blocks.en: Three witnesses have now given their testimony. The first, the canon, showed us the right books; the second, the text, showed us the right words; the third, archaeology, showed us that the events took place in a real world. Now the fourth and final witness rises — and it testifies not to the events, but to the very stage on which they were played: the land itself, with its roads and its rivers and its hills. This witness has a peculiar power that the others do not. Anyone can check it. You do not need a scholar's training in ancient languages, or access to a museum's treasures; you need a map. And the Bible, as we shall see, knows the land it describes the way a man knows his own home — so well that it knows which way is up. The same rule that has guided us throughout still holds: correlation, not proof. Geography cannot prove a miracle, and it will not try. But it can show, with a plainness the humblest reader can feel, that these Scriptures were written by people who stood upon the real ground and knew it under their feet.
blocks.es_reference: Tres testigos han dado ya su testimonio. El primero, el canon, nos mostró los libros correctos; el segundo, el texto, nos mostró las palabras correctas; el tercero, la arqueología, nos mostró que los eventos tuvieron lugar en un mundo real. Ahora se levanta el cuarto y último testigo — y testifica no de los eventos, sino del mismísimo escenario en que fueron representados: la tierra misma, con sus caminos y sus ríos y sus colinas. Este testigo tiene un poder peculiar que los otros no tienen. Cualquiera puede comprobarlo. No necesitas la formación de un erudito en lenguas antiguas, ni acceso a los tesoros de un museo; necesitas un mapa. Y la Biblia, como veremos, conoce la tierra que describe como un hombre conoce su propia casa — tan bien que sabe cuál es la dirección hacia arriba. La misma regla que nos ha guiado por todas partes aún se mantiene: correlación, no prueba. La geografía no puede probar un milagro, y no lo intentará. Pero puede mostrar, con una sencillez que el lector más humilde puede sentir, que estas Escrituras fueron escritas por personas que estuvieron sobre la tierra real y la conocieron bajo sus pies.

blocks.en: 2. Which Way Is Up: The Vertical Bible
blocks.es_reference: 2. Cuál es la Dirección hacia Arriba: La Biblia Vertical

blocks.en: The Bible's directions are not vague poetry; they are the true shape of the land.
blocks.es_reference: Las direcciones de la Biblia no son poesía vaga; son la verdadera forma de la tierra.

blocks.en: Begin with something so simple it is easy to miss. In the Bible, you always go up to Jerusalem, and you always go down from it — no matter which direction you are traveling, north or south, east or west. Why? Because Jerusalem sits high upon the central mountain ridge of the land, and the language simply follows the ground. And hear the Lord's own words in the parable: "A certain man went down from Jerusalem to Jericho." That one small word, down, is exactly right. In only about seventeen miles, the road plunges more than three thousand feet — from the heights of Jerusalem down to Jericho, which lies near the Dead Sea, far below the level of the ocean. It is one of the steepest descents on the face of the earth, and every traveler who has taken it knows the truth of that word "down." The Bible's directions are not vague poetry; they are the true shape of the land. A writer who had never walked that country would not even have known which way was down.
blocks.es_reference: Comienza con algo tan sencillo que es fácil pasarlo por alto. En la Biblia, siempre subes a Jerusalén, y siempre bajas de ella — sin importar en qué dirección viajes, norte o sur, este u oeste. ¿Por qué? Porque Jerusalén se asienta en lo alto de la cordillera montañosa central de la tierra, y el lenguaje simplemente sigue el terreno. Y escucha las propias palabras del Señor en la parábola: "Un hombre descendía de Jerusalén a Jericó." Esa pequeña palabra, descendía, es exactamente correcta. En solo unas diecisiete millas, el camino se precipita más de tres mil pies — desde las alturas de Jerusalén hasta Jericó, que yace cerca del Mar Muerto, muy por debajo del nivel del océano. Es uno de los descensos más empinados de la faz de la tierra, y todo viajero que lo ha tomado conoce la verdad de esa palabra "descendía." Las direcciones de la Biblia no son poesía vaga; son la verdadera forma de la tierra. Un escritor que nunca hubiera caminado ese país no habría sabido siquiera cuál era la dirección hacia abajo.

blocks.en: 3. A Land Below the Sea: The Rift and the Lake
blocks.es_reference: 3. Una Tierra Bajo el Mar: La Hendidura y el Lago

blocks.en: Consider next the great scar that runs down the length of that land: the valley of the Jordan, sinking to the Dead Sea, whose shore is the lowest exposed land elevation on the whole surface of the earth. Set within this deep rift, some seven hundred feet below the level of the ocean, lies the Sea of Galilee — a lake cradled in a bowl of hills. And this shape gives the lake a temper the Gospels know well. When cold air pours down from the surrounding heights and strikes the warm, still air lying over the water, the lake can be lashed, in a matter of minutes and without warning, into a violent and dangerous storm. This is precisely the scene the Gospels paint: the sudden squall that fell upon the boat and terrified even seasoned fishermen, while the Lord slept in the stern. That is not the invention of a distant writer; it is the real weather of a real lake, set down by men who had themselves been drenched and frightened by it. The land and its very skies corroborate the story.
blocks.es_reference: Considera ahora la gran cicatriz que corre a lo largo de esa tierra: el valle del Jordán, hundiéndose hasta el Mar Muerto, cuya orilla es la elevación de tierra expuesta más baja de toda la superficie de la tierra. Situado dentro de esta profunda hendidura, unos setecientos pies bajo el nivel del océano, yace el Mar de Galilea — un lago acunado en un cuenco de colinas. Y esta forma le da al lago un temperamento que los Evangelios conocen bien. Cuando el aire frío se derrama desde las alturas circundantes y golpea el aire cálido y quieto que yace sobre el agua, el lago puede ser azotado, en cuestión de minutos y sin aviso, en una tormenta violenta y peligrosa. Esta es precisamente la escena que pintan los Evangelios: la súbita borrasca que cayó sobre la barca y aterrorizó incluso a pescadores experimentados, mientras el Señor dormía en la popa. Esa no es la invención de un escritor distante; es el clima real de un lago real, puesto por escrito por hombres que ellos mismos habían sido empapados y atemorizados por él. La tierra y sus mismísimos cielos corroboran la historia.

blocks.en: 4. John Knew Jerusalem: Pools and Pavements
blocks.es_reference: 4. Juan Conocía Jerusalén: Estanques y Enlosados

blocks.en: Now turn to the Gospel of John, and to a striking pattern. John names the places of Jerusalem with such exact detail that skeptics once seized upon that detail to accuse him — and one by one, the spade has answered them. John writes that the Pool of Bethesda had five porticoes, five covered colonnades (John five, verse two); the pool was later uncovered, and it had precisely that unusual five-sided colonnaded shape. He names the Pool of Siloam, where the blind man washed and saw (John nine); it too has been excavated. He knows the Pavement, called in Hebrew Gabbatha, where Pilate sat in judgment (John nineteen); he knows Jacob's well at Sychar (John four). This intimate knowledge of the city's waters and stones argues powerfully that the writer knew Jerusalem himself, and knew it before the Roman armies leveled it to the ground in AD 70. It reads as the report of a man who had been there.
blocks.es_reference: Vuélvete ahora al Evangelio de Juan, y a un patrón asombroso. Juan nombra los lugares de Jerusalén con detalle tan exacto que los escépticos una vez se aferraron a ese detalle para acusarlo — y uno por uno, la pala les ha respondido. Juan escribe que el estanque de Betesda tenía cinco pórticos, cinco columnatas cubiertas (Juan cinco, versículo dos); el estanque fue descubierto después, y tenía precisamente esa inusual forma de columnata de cinco lados. Nombra el estanque de Siloé, donde el ciego se lavó y vio (Juan nueve); también ha sido excavado. Conoce el Enlosado, llamado en hebreo Gabata, donde Pilato se sentó a juzgar (Juan diecinueve); conoce el pozo de Jacob en Sicar (Juan cuatro). Este conocimiento íntimo de las aguas y las piedras de la ciudad argumenta poderosamente que el escritor conocía Jerusalén él mismo, y la conocía antes de que los ejércitos romanos la arrasaran hasta el suelo en el 70 d.C. Se lee como el reporte de un hombre que había estado allí.

blocks.en: 5. Luke the Traveler: Every Title Right
blocks.es_reference: 5. Lucas el Viajero: Cada Título Correcto

blocks.en: If John knew Jerusalem, Luke knew the world. Follow Paul across the Roman Empire in the book of Acts, and watch how Luke names the local officials of each place. This is a far harder test than it sounds, for the titles of officials were not uniform; they differed from city to city and province to province, and they changed over time — a snare in which a later forger would surely be caught. Yet in test after test, Luke is not caught out; he gets it right. He calls the rulers of Thessalonica "politarchs" (Acts seventeen) — a title found in no other ancient literature, so that scholars once called it his mistake, until inscriptions bearing that very word were dug up in that very city. He rightly gives the proconsuls of Cyprus and of Achaia, the town clerk of Ephesus, the "first man" of Malta. The scholar Sir William Ramsay began his career trained in a skeptical school of thought that doubted the historical reliability of Acts, but his own years of archaeological fieldwork across Asia Minor gradually persuaded him otherwise, and he came away calling Luke a historian of the first rank. And the account of the shipwreck in Acts twenty-seven reads like a seaman's own logbook, exact in its winds and its soundings and its shores. Luke got the world right because Luke had been in it.
blocks.es_reference: Si Juan conocía Jerusalén, Lucas conocía el mundo. Sigue a Pablo a través del Imperio Romano en el libro de Hechos, y observa cómo Lucas nombra a los funcionarios locales de cada lugar. Esta es una prueba mucho más difícil de lo que suena, pues los títulos de los funcionarios no eran uniformes; diferían de ciudad en ciudad y de provincia en provincia, y cambiaban con el tiempo — una trampa en la que un falsificador posterior seguramente sería atrapado. Sin embargo, prueba tras prueba, Lucas no es sorprendido en falta; acierta. Llama a los gobernantes de Tesalónica "politarcas" (Hechos diecisiete) — un título que no se halla en ninguna otra literatura antigua, de modo que los eruditos una vez lo llamaron su error, hasta que inscripciones que llevaban esa mismísima palabra fueron desenterradas en esa mismísima ciudad. Da correctamente los procónsules de Chipre y de Acaya, el escribano de Éfeso, el "hombre principal" de Malta. El erudito Sir William Ramsay comenzó su carrera formado en una escuela de pensamiento escéptica que dudaba de la fiabilidad histórica de Hechos, pero sus propios años de trabajo arqueológico de campo por Asia Menor lo persuadieron gradualmente de lo contrario, y terminó llamando a Lucas historiador de primer orden. Y el relato del naufragio en Hechos veintisiete se lee como el propio cuaderno de bitácora de un marinero, exacto en sus vientos y sus sondeos y sus costas. Lucas acertó el mundo porque Lucas había estado en él.

blocks.en: 6. A Map in Your Hand: Routes, Distances, Names
blocks.es_reference: 6. Un Mapa en la Mano: Rutas, Distancias, Nombres

blocks.en: Step back now and take in the whole map. The journeys of the Bible run along real roads, and the distances it gives are true. Luke places the village of Emmaus about threescore furlongs from Jerusalem (Luke twenty-four); John places Bethany about fifteen furlongs off (John eleven); and the towns of the Lord's Galilean ministry — Capernaum, Bethsaida, Chorazin — cluster together just where they ought to be, along the northern shore of the lake. Hundreds upon hundreds of places are named in the Scriptures — Bethlehem and Nazareth, the brook Kidron and the Mount of Olives, the garden of Gethsemane — and wherever we are able to locate them today, they answer to the page. This is the promise with which this course began, now made good in the most literal way: you may take a modern map of that land, and follow the footsteps of the Bible across it, and find that the footsteps are true.
blocks.es_reference: Da un paso atrás ahora y contempla todo el mapa. Los viajes de la Biblia corren a lo largo de caminos reales, y las distancias que da son verdaderas. Lucas sitúa la aldea de Emaús a unos sesenta estadios de Jerusalén (Lucas veinticuatro); Juan sitúa Betania a unos quince estadios (Juan once); y los pueblos del ministerio galileo del Señor — Capernaúm, Betsaida, Corazín — se agrupan justo donde deberían estar, a lo largo de la orilla norte del lago. Cientos y cientos de lugares son nombrados en las Escrituras — Belén y Nazaret, el arroyo Cedrón y el Monte de los Olivos, el huerto de Getsemaní — y dondequiera que podemos ubicarlos hoy, responden a la página. Esta es la promesa con que este curso comenzó, ahora cumplida de la manera más literal: puedes tomar un mapa moderno de esa tierra, y seguir las pisadas de la Biblia a través de él, y hallar que las pisadas son verdaderas.

blocks.en: 7. The Mark of the Eyewitness
blocks.es_reference: 7. La Marca del Testigo Ocular

blocks.en: This is the mark of the eyewitness: knowledge too exact to have been faked from far away.
blocks.es_reference: Esta es la marca del testigo ocular: conocimiento demasiado exacto para haber sido falsificado desde lejos.

blocks.en: Now weigh what all of this means, and weigh it by a plain comparison. When writers of a later age, far removed in time and place, sat down to invent gospels and legends about Jesus, they gave themselves away in the geography. They are vague about the land, or they are simply wrong about it, because they had never set foot on it. But the writers of our Bible get it right — right down to the slope of a single road, the shape of a single pool, the title of a single small-town magistrate. And this kind of accuracy is not the sort of thing that can be manufactured from a distance. It is too exact, too incidental, too effortless. It is, in fact, the very mark of the eyewitness — of a man who writes what he has seen — or of one who has drawn faithfully from those who saw. It does not prove the message; that is not its office. But it corroborates, with real weight, that these are the words of men who truly stood where they said they stood, and saw what they said they saw.
blocks.es_reference: Ahora sopesa lo que todo esto significa, y sopésalo por una comparación sencilla. Cuando escritores de una época posterior, muy alejados en tiempo y lugar, se sentaron a inventar evangelios y leyendas sobre Jesús, se delataron en la geografía. Son vagos sobre la tierra, o simplemente están equivocados sobre ella, porque nunca habían puesto pie en ella. Pero los escritores de nuestra Biblia aciertan — hasta la pendiente de un solo camino, la forma de un solo estanque, el título de un solo magistrado de pueblo. Y esta clase de exactitud no es el tipo de cosa que puede fabricarse desde la distancia. Es demasiado exacta, demasiado incidental, demasiado sin esfuerzo. Es, de hecho, la mismísima marca del testigo ocular — de un hombre que escribe lo que ha visto — o de uno que se ha valido fielmente de aquellos que vieron. No prueba el mensaje; ese no es su oficio. Pero corrobora, con peso real, que estas son las palabras de hombres que en verdad estuvieron donde dijeron que estuvieron, y vieron lo que dijeron que vieron.

blocks.en: Eyewitnesses Were People, Not Just a Theory
blocks.es_reference: Los Testigos Oculares Eran Personas, No Solamente una Teoría

blocks.en: The Gospels sometimes preserve the names of people who could be remembered within the first Christian communities. Mark, for example, names Bartimaeus, the blind man healed near Jericho, and identifies Simon of Cyrene as the father of Alexander and Rufus. Such details are easy to pass over, yet they raise an interesting question: why preserve these names unless the people themselves, or their families, were known? Richard Bauckham has argued that named persons can sometimes function as links to eyewitness testimony. The Gospel of John also repeatedly speaks in the language of seeing and bearing witness. This argument should not be exaggerated; a name by itself does not prove every event. But combined with the geographical and historical accuracy already considered in this unit, the personal names fit naturally with a Gospel tradition still connected to people who remembered Jesus and the events surrounding Him.
blocks.es_reference: Los Evangelios a veces conservan los nombres de personas que podían ser recordadas dentro de las primeras comunidades cristianas. Marcos, por ejemplo, nombra a Bartimeo, el ciego sanado cerca de Jericó, e identifica a Simón de Cirene como padre de Alejandro y Rufo. Es fácil pasar por alto estos detalles, pero plantean una pregunta interesante: ¿por qué conservar estos nombres a menos que las personas mismas, o sus familias, fueran conocidas? Richard Bauckham ha argumentado que las personas nombradas pueden funcionar en algunos casos como vínculos con el testimonio ocular. El Evangelio de Juan también habla repetidamente en el lenguaje de ver y dar testimonio. Este argumento no debe exagerarse; un nombre por sí solo no prueba cada acontecimiento. Pero combinado con la exactitud geográfica e histórica ya considerada en esta unidad, los nombres personales encajan naturalmente con una tradición evangélica todavía conectada con personas que recordaban a Jesús y los acontecimientos que lo rodearon.

blocks.en: 8. The Fourth Witness Rests
blocks.es_reference: 8. El Cuarto Testigo Descansa

blocks.en: And so the fourth witness gives its testimony, and it speaks in a tongue that even the simplest believer can understand. Here, it says, is a book that knows the land it tells of; that knows which way is up; that names the pool and the road and the ruler, and gets each one right. It cannot prove to you that the stone was rolled away — no map can reach so far. But it can show you, with your own eyes and a map in your hand, that this Bible is no fable spun in some far-off place; it is sunk deep into real roads, real hills, real stones. The fourth witness rests. And now every witness has been heard — the right books, the right words, the real events, and the real stage. One task alone remains: to gather all their testimony into a single verdict, and to carry it back to the question with which we first set out — can we trust the Bible we hold in our hands? To that final reckoning, and to the certainty it yields, we now come.
blocks.es_reference: Y así el cuarto testigo da su testimonio, y habla en una lengua que aun el creyente más sencillo puede entender. Aquí, dice, hay un libro que conoce la tierra de la que habla; que sabe cuál es la dirección hacia arriba; que nombra el estanque y el camino y el gobernante, y acierta cada uno. No puede probarte que la piedra fue removida — ningún mapa puede alcanzar tan lejos. Pero puede mostrarte, con tus propios ojos y un mapa en la mano, que esta Biblia no es una fábula hilada en algún lugar lejano; está hundida profundamente en caminos reales, colinas reales, piedras reales. El cuarto testigo descansa. Y ahora todo testigo ha sido oído — los libros correctos, las palabras correctas, los eventos reales, y el escenario real. Una sola tarea queda: reunir todo su testimonio en un solo veredicto, y llevarlo de vuelta a la pregunta con que primero partimos — ¿podemos confiar en la Biblia que tenemos en nuestras manos? A esa cuenta final, y a la certeza que produce, ahora llegamos.

sa.prompt: What is the fourth witness, and what is special about how it can be tested?
sa.model: The fourth and final witness is geography — the land itself, the very stage on which the events happened, with its roads, rivers, and hills. What is special is that anyone can test it: you do not need a scholar's training, only a map. The Bible, we find, knows the land the way a man knows his own home, and the same rule holds — correlation, not proof.

sa.prompt: Explain how the Bible's "up/down" language matches the real topography, using Jerusalem and Jericho.
sa.model: In the Bible one always goes up to Jerusalem and down from it, whatever the compass direction, because Jerusalem sits high on the central ridge. The Lord's parable says a man went down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and that is exact: the road drops over three thousand feet in about seventeen miles, from the heights of Jerusalem to Jericho near the Dead Sea, one of the steepest descents on earth. The Bible's directions are the true shape of the land.

sa.prompt: Why is the Sea of Galilee prone to sudden storms, and how does this match the Gospels?
sa.model: The Sea of Galilee sits some seven hundred feet below the level of the ocean, ringed by hills, so that cold air spilling down the slopes collides with the warm air over the water and whips it, without warning, into violent storms. This is exactly what the Gospels describe — the sudden squall that terrified seasoned fishermen while Jesus slept. The meteorology of a real lake is reported by men who had been soaked by it.

sa.prompt: How does John's precise knowledge of Jerusalem support his account?
sa.model: The Gospel of John names places with such precision that skeptics once used them against him, and the spade has answered. He says the Pool of Bethesda had five porticoes, and the pool was found with exactly that colonnaded shape; he names the Pool of Siloam, now excavated, and the Pavement called Gabbatha. Such exact knowledge argues the writer knew Jerusalem intimately, before the Romans leveled it in AD 70 — the report of one who had been there.

sa.prompt: Why is Luke's naming of local officials in Acts remarkable, and who was Ramsay?
sa.model: As Paul crosses the empire, Luke names the local officials, and their titles differed from city to city and changed with the years, a trap for any forger. Yet Luke is right every time: the politarchs of Thessalonica, once called an error and then found on inscriptions; the proconsuls of Cyprus and Achaia; the town clerk of Ephesus. The scholar William Ramsay began doubting Luke and ended by calling him a historian of the first rank.

sa.prompt: Give examples of the Bible's accuracy in routes, distances, and place-names.
sa.model: The journeys of the Bible trace real roads, and the distances match: Luke sets Emmaus about threescore furlongs from Jerusalem, and John sets Bethany about fifteen furlongs away. The towns of Jesus's ministry cluster just where they should, around the northern shore of Galilee. Hundreds of towns and springs and landmarks are named — Bethlehem, Nazareth, the brook Kidron, the Mount of Olives — and where we can find them, they fit the page.

sa.prompt: Explain the "mark of the eyewitness" argument from geography.
sa.model: When later writers, generations removed, invented gospels about Jesus, they betrayed themselves in the geography — vague about the land or plainly mistaken, because they had never seen it. But the canonical writers get it right, down to the slope of a road, the name of a pool, and the title of a magistrate. This exact, incidental, effortless knowledge is the mark of the eyewitness, or of one who drew from eyewitnesses. It does not prove the message, but powerfully corroborates that these men stood where they said.

sa.prompt: Does geography prove the Bible's message? State the unit's position.
sa.model: No — the rule is correlation, not proof. Geography cannot prove that the tomb was empty; no map can reach a miracle. But it powerfully corroborates that the writers stood where they said they stood and saw what they said they saw, since their knowledge of the real land is too exact to have been faked from far away. It shows the Bible is no fable told from a distance, but a record rooted in real roads and hills and stones.

sa.prompt: What does the witness of geography especially allow the ordinary believer to do?
sa.model: It especially allows the ordinary reader to test the Bible himself, with a map, without a scholar's training. He can trace the road from Jerusalem to Jericho and feel the descent, or stand at the Pool of Siloam. This is a witness the humblest believer can weigh with his own eyes: here is a book that knows the land it describes, that knows which way is up, and names the pool and the road and the ruler and gets them right.

sa.prompt: In your own words, why is a book's exact knowledge of geography evidence that it is trustworthy?
sa.model: Because a writer inventing a story from a distant land and a later century cannot help getting the geography wrong, while one who truly knew the land gets it right without effort. When a book names the pool, the road, the slope, and the ruler correctly, down to incidental detail, it shows the author stood on the real ground. This exact knowledge is a mark of the eyewitness and corroborates his trustworthiness, though it is correlation, not proof of the message.
